A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

experimental data are available to describe the behaviour of many radionuclids in fruit plants, but that there is a lack of data on the behaviour of many of the radionuclid isotopes in fruits, particularly for those isotopes of importance to the public health.
experimental studies on fruit plants have provided a better understanding of the behaviour of radionuclide contaminants in the fruit system and have improved the reliability of dose assessment.

, while experimental studies are important to fill gaps in the knowledge of the behaviour of radionuclide in fruits and to validate models, they are expensive and time consuming and, in many cases, are not sufficient to provide reliable estimates for risk assessment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
experimental studies are a powerful tool to investigate processes and parameters of radionuclide transfer in fruit plants.
there are still many gaps in our knowledge on the transfer of radionuclide from the soil and the atmosphere to fruit, and on translocation and carryover of radionuclidesto fruit.
there is a need to develop a better understanding of the processes of deposition, uptake and transfer to fruit of gaseous radionuclide species and of radionuclide transfer from soil to fruit.
